There is a particular kind of permission in being told you may write about whatever you want—like being handed a key to a house with no doors, only windows, and being informed that you are allowed to look out in any direction you please. I think I will look at rain.

Not the dramatic kind that arrives with thunder and cinematic urgency, but the slow, democratic rain that falls for three hours without announcement. It lands on the asphalt of streets that have just begun to smell like wet stone and old leaves. It lands on the green plastic of a park bench, turning it briefly into a darker, more serious color, as if the bench itself has just had a thought. It lands on the glass of a coffee shop window, blurring the world outside so that the streetlamps become soft, orange coins, and the people walking become semi-transparent, temporary.

I like this rain because it does not demand a reaction. It is not a crisis; it is a texture. And when you are granted the freedom to write freely, I think the best thing you can do is pay attention to textures rather than plots. You can notice that rain has different weights. It sounds like a single continuous note when it hits a flat roof, but on a metal awning, it becomes a rhythm—almost musical, a percussion section made of weather. On an open window screen, it becomes individual drops, each one a tiny decision to fall.

I have been thinking lately about the happiness of not being useful. We live in a world that asks everything to be optimized, narrated, or monetized, but the open prompt—*write whatever you want*—is a small rebellion against that. It says: this does not need to become a product. It can remain an experience. You can write about the way your left hand sits differently on a mug in the morning, or about the sound of a distant train that you cannot see, or about a color you remember from childhood that you no longer have a name for.

If I must choose a subject, I choose the feeling of liminal spaces. The doorways between inside and outside. The exact second when the sky shifts from blue to gray, not because it intends to storm, but because it is simply becoming more honest. The moment after you finish a conversation and before you start the next one, when you are just a body with air moving through it.

But maybe that is too abstract. Let me try to be more specific. I am thinking of a particular street I have walked many times, a street with broad box trees that drop their leaves in October with a kind of abandon, as if they have decided to stop holding on. After rain, those leaves lie flat and dark, and the street becomes a quilt of green, brown, and silver. The air is cooler, but not cold—just different, as if someone has changed the lighting in a room and you have not yet adjusted your eyes.

When I write freely, I want to write like that rain: not insisting on one direction, but available to every surface it touches. I want to be unhurried. I want to allow the sentence to wander, because sometimes the wandering is the only honest thing about it.

So I will end not with a conclusion, but with a question left open, like a window. If you could write about anything right now—truly anything—would you write about a feeling you have not named yet? Would you describe the sound of your own breathing at this exact second? Would you invent a color?

I hope you do. I hope you let yourself be that unproductive, that spacious, that free. Because the world has enough answers. It could use more open windows.
